content: Globally, children under the age of 15 account for approximately 12% of new tuberculosis (TB) cases. However, they represent 16% of the estimated 1.4 million deaths caused by TB, indicating a disproportionately high mortality rate in this age group. This underscores the urgent need for strategies to improve TB case detection in children and to identify those who do not have active TB but may benefit from preventive treatment. Systematic screening for TB in high-risk groups is one such strategy. The objective of this study was to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of various screening tests for detecting active pulmonary TB in children. These tests included the presence of one or more TB-related symptoms (or combinations of symptoms), chest radiography (CXR), Xpert MTB/RIF, Xpert Ultra, and combinations of these methods. The study focused on specific high-risk groups, including children who are close contacts of individuals with infectious TB (e.g., household or school contacts), children living with HIV, children with pneumonia, malnourished children, children with a history of TB, and children in high TB burden settings. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of six databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, and Embase, up to February 14, 2020. They included cross-sectional and cohort studies where at least 75% of participants were under 15 years old. Eligible studies were those designed for TB screening rather than diagnosis. The reference standards used were microbiological reference standards (MRS) and composite reference standards (CRS), which could include symptoms and CXR findings. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the quality of the studies using the QUADAS-2 tool. Symptom screens were grouped into categories based on similar combinations of symptoms, such as one or more of cough, fever, or poor weight gain and one or more of cough, fever, or decreased playfulness. A positive screen was defined as the presence of at least one symptom. A bivariate model was used to estimate pooled sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and analyses were conducted separately based on the reference standard. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review included 19 studies that evaluated various screening methods. These included single symptoms (15 studies, 10,097 participants), combinations of symptoms (12 studies, 29,889 participants), CXR (10 studies, 7,146 participants), and Xpert MTB/RIF (2 studies, 787 participants). No studies assessed Xpert Ultra. For 16 of the studies (84%), the risk of bias in the reference standard domain was unclear due to concerns about incorporation bias. However, the risk of bias in other quality domains was generally low. Symptom Screening (verified by CRS): In children who were TB contacts, the presence of one or more symptoms (cough, fever, or poor weight gain) had a pooled sensitivity of 89% (95% CI 52% to 98%) and a pooled specificity of 69% (95% CI 51% to 83%) based on four studies. For every 1,000 children screened, where 50 have pulmonary TB, 339 would test positive, of whom 294 (87%) would not have TB (false positives). Meanwhile, 661 would test negative, of whom five (1%) would have TB (false negatives). In children under five years of age (inpatient or outpatient), the presence of one or more symptoms (cough, fever, or decreased playfulness) had a sensitivity ranging from 64% to 76% and a specificity ranging from 37% to 77%. For every 1,000 children screened, where 50 have pulmonary TB, 251 to 636 would test positive, of whom 219 to 598 (87% to 94%) would not have TB. Meanwhile, 364 to 749 would test negative, of whom 12 to 18 (2% to 3%) would have TB. In children living with HIV, the World Health Organization (WHO) four-symptom screen (cough, fever, poor weight gain, or TB close contact) had a pooled sensitivity of 61% (95% CI 58% to 64%) and a pooled specificity of 94% (95% CI 86% to 98%). For every 1,000 symptom screens, where 50 are on children with pulmonary TB, 88 would test positive, of whom 57 (65%) would not have TB. Meanwhile, 912 would test negative, of whom 19 (2%) would have TB. Chest Radiography (CXR, verified by CRS): In children who were TB contacts, CXR showing any abnormality had a pooled sensitivity of 87% (95% CI 75% to 93%) and a pooled specificity of 99% (95% CI 68% to 100%) based on eight studies. For every 1,000 children screened, where 50 have pulmonary TB, 63 would test positive, of whom 19 (30%) would not have TB. Meanwhile, 937 would test negative, of whom six (1%) would have TB. Xpert MTB/RIF (verified by MRS): In inpatient or outpatient settings, Xpert MTB/RIF had a sensitivity of 43% to 100% and a specificity of 99% to 100% based on two studies. For every 1,000 children screened, where 50 have pulmonary TB, 31 to 69 would test positive, of whom 9 to 19 (28% to 29%) would not have TB. Meanwhile, 931 to 969 would test negative, of whom 0 to 28 (0% to 3%) would have TB. The studies often assessed more symptoms than those included in the index test, and definitions of symptoms varied. These differences complicated data aggregation and may have influenced the accuracy estimates. Additionally, the use of symptoms and CXR as part of the CRS introduced incorporation bias, potentially leading to overestimation of sensitivity and specificity. Conclusions: In children who are TB contacts or living with HIV, screening tests using symptoms or CXR may be useful. However, the review was limited by design issues with the index tests and incorporation bias in the reference standards. For Xpert MTB/RIF, there was insufficient evidence to determine its accuracy as a screening tool. Prospective evaluations of TB screening tests in children are needed to clarify their utility. In the meantime, screening strategies should be pragmatic to address the persistent gaps in TB prevention and case detection, particularly in resource-limited settings.
